title: Your AI Receptionist Might Actually Pay for Itself (Here's What You Need to Know)
excerpt: AI receptionists are everywhere right now, but the real question isn't whether they work — it's whether they make sense for YOUR business.

content.text: So there's this thing happening right now where everybody and their cousin is talking about AI receptionists, and honestly? I get why. The math is actually starting to make sense. But before you get excited and swap out your current phone setup, let's talk about what's really going on here and whether it's actually a move you should make.
What's Changed (And Why Everyone's Suddenly Talking About This)

AI phone agents used to be a total pain to set up. You needed a tech person, someone who could code, months of tweaking. Now? The barrier to entry has basically vanished. Companies are building these tools so that regular business owners can actually use them without needing a degree in computer science. That's the real shift.

And here's the part that actually matters to you: people are starting to measure whether these things actually work. Not just "does it exist," but "does it save me money and make my customers happier?" The early data is saying yes — but with conditions.

items: A human receptionist costs you roughly $30,000–$40,000 a year, plus benefits, plus training, plus the fact that they need days off
A good AI receptionist system runs $500–$2,000 a month depending on call volume
The payback period? For most small businesses handling 100+ calls a month, we're talking 3–6 months before you're actually ahead
But here's the kicker: ROI varies wildly by industry. Service businesses (HVAC, dental, legal) see faster returns than retail

content.text: Most businesses are paying $15–$50 per user per month for their entire VoIP system right now. An AI receptionist typically sits on top of that, not replacing it.

Real talk: this isn't for everyone. You're a good fit if you're getting hammered with calls about appointment scheduling, basic questions, or customer intake stuff. You're not a good fit if your business relies on nuanced conversations or complex problem-solving on the first call.

Also — and this matters — your customers need to be okay with talking to a robot first. Some industries? No problem. Other industries? You might lose a customer or two before you get used to it. Think about your specific crowd.

content.label: Intecha's Take
content.text: Don't buy this because everyone's doing it. Do a real audit: How many calls come in that could be handled by automation? What's your current cost per call (including your time)? How much would you actually save? Do the math first, then decide. And if you do move forward, start with a free trial or low-cost test run. These tools are getting better every month — rushing into a year-long contract is the move that bites people.
The bottom line: AI receptionists are actually becoming a legitimate business tool, not just a neat gadget. But you need to know your own numbers first. That's always the rule.
